extracted.intended_audience: public company executives, corporate communications staff, general counsel, compliance officers, investor-relations professionals
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for public companies on avoiding Regulation FD violations arising from social media posts (including executives' personal accounts) and on required corrective steps and policies. Focuses on what constitutes a violation, acceptable social media use, timing for corrective disclosures, policy elements, training, and enforcement risks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Selective disclosure of material nonpublic information
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation FD prohibits public companies from selectively disclosing material nonpublic information to certain individuals, including investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Material nonpublic information disclosed on social media (including posts on a CEO’s personal accounts) that is seen by investors can be treated as selective disclosure. The SEC may charge companies for selectively disclosing material nonpublic information even where the disclosure occurred via an executive’s personal account or through a third-party public relations firm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement to make public disclosure as soon as reasonably practicable after unintentional selective disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: When unintentional selective disclosure is made, Regulation FD requires that public disclosure follow as soon as reasonably practicable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failing to make a prompt public disclosure after discovering selective disclosure can itself be the basis for an SEC charge (the firm was charged for failing to make the “required prompt, public disclosure”). The firm in the example waited seven days and was charged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timing for corrective action — disclose within 24 hours or next business day
rubrics_metrics.description: Public companies must undertake prompt corrective action by disclosing the information within 24 hours or within the next business day of discovering that information has been selectively disclosed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Removing the offending post is not sufficient; companies are expected to make a public disclosure within the 24-hour/next-business-day window after discovery. The blog highlights this as a best-practice (and as a standard the SEC looks to in enforcement).

rubrics_metrics.name: Social media is acceptable for company announcements only if investors are alerted and accounts are unrestricted
rubrics_metrics.description: Social media can be an acceptable place for company announcements so long as (1) investors are all alerted that information may be disseminated that way and (2) the social media accounts are not restricted to only some investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cites SEC guidance/press release that the company must alert investors that it will use social media for disclosures and ensure accounts are broadly accessible (not restricted to a subset of investors). Without those conditions, a social-media post may constitute selective disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policies must cover executives’ private social media accounts
rubrics_metrics.description: Public companies should ensure their Regulation FD policies cover public company executives’ private social media accounts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should explicitly address use of personal/professional accounts by executives (and when those accounts constitute channels for company disclosure). The example shows a PR firm posted to the CEO’s personal X and LinkedIn accounts, triggering the issue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Establish or review Regulation FD policies with accurate rules and restrictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Public companies should establish or review their Regulation FD policies to ensure they provide accurate rules and restrictions on disclosure of material nonpublic information.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policies should be detailed and current, address roles/responsibilities, specify permissible channels (including social media), and define procedures for handling inadvertent disclosures and required corrective steps. Regular review is recommended given rising SEC focus.

rubrics_metrics.name: Include quiet-period rules prohibiting spokespersons from discussing results
rubrics_metrics.description: Regulation FD policies should include quiet-period rules (e.g., between quarter-end and filing) that bar company spokespersons from discussing financial or operational results.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even where quiet periods and prohibitions exist, violations can still occur; companies should ensure enforcement of quiet-period rules and that all employees and third parties understand and follow them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train employees with corporate-communication responsibilities on Regulation FD compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Companies should train all employees with corporate-communication responsibilities on compliance with Regulation FD.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training was a settlement requirement in the example (company agreed to train such employees). Regular, documented training helps prevent violations and demonstrates proactive compliance to regulators.

rubrics_metrics.name: Manage third-party/PR firm communications for compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: Third parties (e.g., public relations firms) posting on behalf of the company or executives can create Regulation FD exposure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Companies must ensure vendors and PR firms understand and follow the company’s Regulation FD policies and disclosure protocols; contractually require compliance and oversight where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Removal of posts does not eliminate liability; corrective disclosure still required
rubrics_metrics.description: Removing an offending social-media post quickly does not by itself satisfy the obligation to make a prompt public disclosure after selective disclosure.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the example the PR firm removed the posts within 30 minutes, but because the company failed to make the required prompt public disclosure, the SEC charged the company. Companies should treat removal as only the first step and promptly make the required public disclosure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential enforcement consequences — charges, cease-and-desist, civil penalties, settlement terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The SEC can bring charges for Regulation FD violations and related Exchange Act violations; settlements can include cease-and-desist orders, civil penalties, and mandated compliance steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In the discussed settlement the company consented to cease-and-desist, paid a $200,000 civil penalty, and agreed to training. Awareness of these consequences should inform policy design and incident response planning.

rubrics_metrics.name: SEC enforcement of Regulation FD is increasing — monitor and update compliance programs
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Regulation FD enforcement has been rare since adoption, recent actions demonstrate the SEC is starting to focus more on disclosure compliance and fairness to investors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public companies should monitor SEC enforcement trends, review prior related enforcement actions, and update policies and training accordingly to mitigate enforcement risk.
